1914 The phantoms flit before our dazzled eyes, Glory and honour, wrath and righteousness, The agèd phantoms in their bloodstained dress, Vultures that fill the world with ravenous cries, Swarming about the rock where, chained apart, In age-long pain Prometheus finds no rest From the divine flame burning in his breast, And vultures tearing at a human heart. Not yet the blessed hours on golden wings Bring to the crucified their sure relief, Deeper and deeper grows the ancient grief, Blackest of all intolerable things. Eternal Rebel, sad, and old, and blind, Bound with a chain enslaved by every one Of the dark gods who hide the summer sun, Yet art thou still the saviour of mankind. Free soul of fire, break down their chains and bars, Drive out those unclean phantoms of the brain, Till every living thing be friends again, And our lost earth true comrade to the stars.

Keywords: The, Glory, Vultures

outputs.L1:
**1914**

The phantoms flit before our dazzled eyes—  
Glory and honour, wrath and righteousness—  
The agèd phantoms in their bloodstained dress,  
Vultures that fill the world with ravenous cries,  
Swarming about the rock where, chained apart,  
In age-long pain Prometheus finds no rest  
From the divine flame burning in his breast,  
And vultures tearing at a human heart.

Not yet the blessed hours, on golden wings,  
Bring to the crucified their sure relief;  
Deeper and deeper grows the ancient grief,  
Blackest of all intolerable things.

Eternal Rebel—sad, and old, and blind—  
Bound with a chain, enslaved by every one  
Of the dark gods who hide the summer sun,  
Yet art thou still the saviour of mankind.

Free soul of fire, break down their chains and bars;  
Drive out those unclean phantoms of the brain,  
Till every living thing be friends again,  
And our lost earth true comrade to the stars.
outputs.L2:
**1914**

Before our blinded gaze, old spectres wheel—  
Honour and glory, justice and rage—  
Ancient shapes clothed in garments soaked with blood,  
Like hungry vultures whose cries engulf the earth.  
They gather around the lonely stone  
Where Prometheus has endured endless torment,  
The sacred fire still blazing within his chest  
While beaks rip ceaselessly at his human heart.

The merciful hours have not yet arrived  
On radiant wings to rescue the crucified;  
Instead, primeval sorrow deepens,  
More unbearable and dark than anything else.  
Prometheus—eternal rebel, weary, sightless, and aged—  
Remains shackled and subject to all  
The shadowy gods who conceal the summer sun,  
Yet he continues to be humanity’s deliverer.

Fiery and unconquered spirit, shatter every prison;  
Banish these foul illusions from the mind  
Until all living beings become companions once more,  
And our estranged earth rejoins the stars as a friend.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents glory, honour, wrath, and righteousness not as noble ideals, but as ancient, bloodstained phantoms that perpetuate the horrors of war. These forces haunt humanity, disguising violence as virtue and driving generation after generation toward conflict and destruction.

At the centre of the poem stands Prometheus, a symbol of humanity’s capacity to endure suffering while preserving the divine flame within. His torment is ancient and unrelieved, and the absence of comfort intensifies a grief portrayed as the most intolerable of all evils. Yet his suffering does not defeat him. Although he is chained and punished by oppressive gods, Prometheus remains the eternal rebel and the saviour of humankind, resisting tyranny for the sake of human freedom and enlightenment.

The poem ultimately becomes an appeal to the liberating spirit of fire. This free and transformative force is called upon to break both mental and physical chains, destroying the systems of oppression that imprison human bodies and minds. Through this liberation, harmony may be restored among all living beings, allowing friendship to replace conflict and division. The poem therefore imagines a final reconciliation on a cosmic scale, in which Earth is reunited with the stars and humanity recovers its place within a free, interconnected universe.
outputs.L4:
The poem portrays the outbreak of war in 1914 as a catastrophe that exposes the emptiness of patriotic ideals such as glory, honor, and righteousness. To deepen this critique, it draws on the myth of Prometheus, the Titan who defied the gods by giving fire to humanity and was condemned to endless torment. His suffering becomes a symbol of the pain endured by humankind, while his courage and resistance represent the possibility of deliverance.

Against the language used to justify war, the poem sets the brutal reality of destruction, sacrifice, and grief. Ideas that appear noble in speeches and slogans are revealed as dangerous illusions when they lead people to violence. The true burden of these beliefs falls on ordinary human beings, whose suffering continues long after claims of victory or heroism have lost their meaning. Like Prometheus, humanity is shown as bound and tormented by powerful forces, including authority, false ideals, hatred, and blind obedience.

Yet the poem does not present Prometheus merely as a victim. His rebellious spirit offers a model of hope. By resisting unjust power and acting for the benefit of humankind, he embodies the courage needed to reject the destructive beliefs that sustain conflict. His symbolic fire can therefore be understood not only as knowledge, but also as moral awakening: the ability to recognize deception, challenge oppression, and imagine a different future.

The poem ultimately calls for liberation from the chains of militarism, fanaticism, and false heroism. Humanity can be saved only by abandoning the ideas that divide people and condemn them to repeated suffering. In their place, the poem affirms peace, fellowship, compassion, and harmony. Prometheus’s defiance thus becomes a symbol of humanity’s enduring capacity to resist destruction and rebuild a world founded on shared dignity rather than violence.
outputs.L5:
## The Glory of Vultures

The vultures circled above the silent valley, their dark wings cutting across the burning sky. To those below, they seemed like symbols of ruin, waiting patiently for life to surrender. Yet there was a strange glory in their flight—a calm, effortless command of the wind.

They did not create death; they answered it. By clearing what had fallen, they returned strength to the earth and made space for life to begin again. Misunderstood and unwelcome, the vultures carried out an ancient duty.

Their glory was not beautiful in the ordinary sense. It was harsher, quieter, and necessary: the glory of survival, renewal, and balance.

counterfactuals.output:
War broke: and now the Winter of the world
With perishing great darkness closes in.
The foul tornado, centred at Berlin,
Is over all the width of Europe whirled,
Rending the sails of progress. Rent or furled
Are all Art’s ensigns. Verse wails. Now begin
Famines of thought and feeling. Love’s wine’s thin.
The grain of human Autumn rots, down-hurled.

For after Spring had bloomed in early Greece,
And Summer blazed her glory out with Rome,
An Autumn softly fell, a harvest-home,
A slow grand age, and rich with all increase.
But now, for us, wild Winter, and the need
Of sowings for new Spring, and blood for seed.
